## Chloride as a conservative thermal-water tracer

Steamboat Hills' thermal water is a Na-Cl-dominated fluid; meteoric
(background) water in the same area is dilute and comparatively richer in
Ca and Mg. Chloride behaves conservatively in this system -- it is not
appreciably removed or added by mineral precipitation/dissolution or gas
loss during ascent and mixing -- which is what makes it usable as a
tracer of thermal-water fraction in any sample, and, by mass balance
against stream discharge, as an estimate of total thermal-water discharge
from the system [@sorey1992; @sorey2008; @sorey2017]. This project's
entire conductivity-logger workstream (Chapter 3) exists because specific
conductance is a cheap, continuous, field-deployable proxy for chloride
concentration -- not because conductance is itself the quantity of
scientific interest.

## Major-ion chemistry: what each analyte tells us

| Analyte | Role in this system |
|---|---|
| Cl | The primary conservative tracer (above). |
| Na, K | Track with Cl in the real thermal end-member (strong positive correlation, r >= 0.89 in this project's own data); also the basis of Na/K geothermometry (below). |
| SO4 | Also strongly correlated with Cl/Na/K here -- a secondary conservative-ish tracer, though sulfate can be affected by anhydrite/gypsum equilibria at high enough concentration (tracked via saturation index, below). |
| Ca, Mg | Behave oppositely to the Cl/Na/K group in this system (negative correlation) -- generally track a separate, more dilute/rock-reacted water-rock interaction signature (e.g. the Ca-Na-Cl "diluted and reacted" hydrochemical facies identified in this project's own clustering work). |
| Alkalinity (as HCO3) | Drives carbonate mineral saturation (calcite/dolomite/aragonite SI, below); a genuine, project-wide unit-consistency effort (documented in `AGENTS.md` Sessions 15-16) was needed to put every source's alkalinity on the same HCO3-mass basis before this was usable. |
| B, Li, F | Minor conservative-ish tracers used for cross-checks (e.g. the Cl/B ratio stability test in Chapter 4) rather than as primary tracers themselves. |
| SiO2 | The basis of quartz/chalcedony geothermometry (below); behaves less conservatively than Na/K on the ascent-to-discharge path in this system (see the geothermometer-divergence discussion, Chapter 4). |

## Charge balance and saturation index

Every water analysis used in this project's PHREEQC modeling is first
screened for internal consistency via the standard charge-balance-error
statistic:

$$
\text{CBE\%} = \frac{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} - \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}}
{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} + \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}} \times 100
$$

A sample passing within +/-5% is treated as analytically reliable enough
to model further. Real charge-balance-error work in this project (see
`notebooks/06_phreeqc_geochemical_modeling.qmd`, `notebooks/08_statistical_synthesis.qmd`)
found this number was initially dominated by a missing-alkalinity data gap
rather than real analytical error -- median imbalance dropped from ~60% to
~0.7% once alkalinity was correctly ingested project-wide.

The mineral saturation index quantifies how far a water is from
equilibrium with a given mineral:

$$
SI = \log_{10}\left(\frac{IAP}{K_{sp}}\right)
$$

where $IAP$ is the ion activity product computed from the sample's real
speciated chemistry and $K_{sp}$ is that mineral's temperature-dependent
solubility product. $SI = 0$ is equilibrium; $SI > 0$ implies
supersaturation (a tendency to precipitate, i.e. scale); $SI < 0$ implies
undersaturation (a tendency to dissolve). This project's real thermal
samples sit near quartz/chalcedony equilibrium and mildly-to-moderately
supersaturated with respect to calcite/dolomite -- a real, geologically
meaningful, not merely numerical, result.

## PHREEQC and its thermodynamic databases

**PHREEQC** [@phreeqc] is a widely-used, open-source geochemical modeling
program that solves aqueous speciation, mineral saturation, mixing, and
inverse mass-balance problems from a water analysis and a chosen
thermodynamic database. This project runs the real, standalone PHREEQC 3
executable (not an R re-implementation) via `system2()`, so every result
is exactly what the reference software itself would produce.

Five thermodynamic databases are registered in this project
(`scripts/phreeqc/utils_phreeqc.R`), each with different strengths, and
one is auto-recommended per sample based on its temperature and total
dissolved solids:

| Database | When it's used here |
|---|---|
| `llnl.dat` | The default for real, high-temperature (>100C) Steamboat thermal samples -- has the broadest high-temperature mineral/aqueous-species coverage of the five. |
| `sit.dat` (SIT) | Used as a fallback for large batches of dilute, low-temperature background samples (e.g. the 225 NDEP wells) when `llnl.dat` fails to converge on that population -- this fallback logic was built specifically because it was needed in practice, not speculatively. |
| `pitzer.dat` | Registered for high-ionic-strength brines; not yet exercised by this project's real samples, which are not brine-strength. |
| `phreeqc.dat` | The minimal/default PHREEQC database; used mainly in this project's synthetic self-tests. |
| `wateq4f.dat` | Registered as an alternative for trace-metal-focused speciation; not yet the primary choice for any real batch here. |

## Geothermometry: two independent, and divergent, temperature estimates

**Activity-based Na/K geothermometers** estimate the deep reservoir
temperature a water last equilibrated with, from the ratio of sodium to
potassium activity (not raw concentration -- PHREEQC's own computed
activities are used):

Giggenbach (1988) [@giggenbach1988]:
$$
T_{\text{Gigg}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1390}{1.75 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15
$$

Fournier (1979) [@fournier1979]:
$$
T_{\text{Four}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1217}{1.483 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15
$$

**Silica (quartz/chalcedony) geothermometry** instead uses dissolved
SiO2's own temperature-dependent solubility, computed here via a real
PHREEQC temperature sweep (25-300C by 25C steps) rather than a fixed
empirical equation, so the crossing temperature where SI = 0 for each
mineral is read directly from real modeled equilibria.

For this project's real thermal samples, Na/K estimates (154-256C)
systematically and substantially exceed quartz/chalcedony estimates
(52-127C). This is not treated as a contradiction to explain away: silica
re-equilibrates toward ambient conditions faster than the Na/K ratio does
as water cools and dilutes on its way to discharge, so the two
geothermometers are expected to diverge exactly this way for a cooling,
diluting outflow path -- the divergence itself is evidence for that
process, not a modeling error.

## Two-end-member mixing and inverse modeling

The simplest defensible model of how a sample's chemistry relates to a
real thermal and a real meteoric end-member is conservative linear
mixing on a tracer (chloride):

$$
f_{\text{thermal}} = \frac{C_{\text{obs}} - C_{\text{meteoric}}}{C_{\text{thermal}} - C_{\text{meteoric}}}
$$

This project computes this fraction directly, then builds a real PHREEQC
`MIX` block combining the two end-member solutions at that fraction and
compares PHREEQC's full predicted speciation/SI (which is not required to
behave conservatively) against the sample's own observed chemistry -- a
genuine test of the two-end-member hypothesis, not just an arithmetic
ratio. See Chapter 4 for the real result of this run against real
Steamboat samples.

PHREEQC's `INVERSE_MODELING` keyword goes further, solving simultaneously
for mixing fractions *and* mineral mass transfer (e.g. how much calcite
would need to dissolve or precipitate along a flow path) within stated
elemental uncertainty bounds. **A methodological note, in the interest of
transparency**: this project's automated parser for PHREEQC's inverse-
modeling text output has a known, real gap (discovered while preparing
this manuscript) -- it correctly finds that a real run produced a feasible
solution, but has not yet correctly extracted that solution's actual
mineral-mass-transfer numbers from the raw output text. This is flagged
explicitly in `ROADMAP.md` as a concrete near-term fix, and no invented or
placeholder numbers are presented here in its place.

## An important modeling principle: chemistry first, spatial connectivity second

A recurring design decision in this project is worth stating explicitly,
since it will matter more once a 3D geologic model (Leapfrog) and
groundwater flow model (MODFLOW) exist: **a defensible mixing or
reaction-path model is built from real, conservative-tracer chemistry --
which samples are genuinely distinct, credible end-members -- not from map
proximity.** Two samples that are spatially close are not necessarily
hydraulically connected, and two that are far apart are not necessarily
unconnected. Independent spatial/structural evidence (fault traces,
hydraulic heads, a 3D lithologic model) should be used to *test or refine*
which chemically-plausible end-members are worth pairing, not to define
the chemistry itself. The real mixing model already run in this project
(Chapter 4) follows this logic: its two end-members were chosen because
they are chemically distinct (Cl = 815 vs. 45 mg/L), not because they are
near each other on a map.

## Gas geochemistry (built, not yet run on real Steamboat gas samples)

A multicomponent CO2-H2-H2S-CH4 gas geothermometer following D'Amore &
Panichi (1980) [@damore1980] is implemented and cross-validated against
real, published Mariner & Janik (1995) values for well 23-5 (agreement
within 0.3C across all four of their sampling dates) -- confirming the
implementation is correct, independent of whether this project has its
own real gas chemistry to apply it to yet (it does not, as of this
writing).

## R statistical methods used throughout this work

Beyond PHREEQC itself, this project uses standard, appropriately-chosen
statistical methods rather than a single default test everywhere:
Shapiro-Wilk normality testing and `fitdistrplus`-based distribution
comparison for PHREEQC output distributions; Welch/Student two-sample
t-tests and Kruskal-Wallis/pairwise Wilcoxon rank tests depending on
whether normality holds; a significance-tested Pearson correlation matrix
and PCA for multivariate ion relationships; hierarchical (Ward) clustering
cross-checked against a Gaussian-mixture fit for hydrochemical facies;
linear mixed-effects models (`lme4`) where repeated sampling of the same
well/location needs to be accounted for rather than pooled naively; and
nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals where a real sample size is
too small (n = 7-8) to trust a classical CLT-based interval. See
`notebooks/07_historical_context_sorey1992.qmd` and
`notebooks/08_statistical_synthesis.qmd` for every real result these
methods have produced against this project's actual data, paired with the
exact code that computed each one.
